  Line or code reference: `FAILING_TESTS_JSON="$(python3 ... || echo '{"names":[],"files":[]}')"` (around the new failing-tests extraction block)
  Problem: The fallback JSON emitted when the Python helper crashes lacks the new `pairs` key. Downstream consumers that read `failing_tests.pairs` via `failing.get("pairs") or []` still tolerate the omission, so this is benign in practice, but it is an asymmetric fallback shape that has to be remembered at every read site.
  Why it fails at runtime: It does not actually fail at runtime today (every read uses `or []`), but the shape drift between the success path (`{names, files, pairs}`) and the failure path (`{names, files}`) creates a future-bug trap if a new caller reads `failing_tests["pairs"]` directly instead of via `get(..., [])`.

  Line or code reference: `_cmd_heal_scope` render branch (`matches = [path for path in matches if isinstance(name, str) and path in reported_for_name.get(name, set())]`)
  Problem: The `isinstance(name, str)` guard inside the list comprehension is dead defensive code. `name` was just produced by iterating over `failing.get("names") or []`, and `_heal_test_files_for_names` already validates `isinstance(name, str)` before doing the git grep — so when `len(matches) > 1` is reached, `name` is guaranteed to be a string already.
  Why it fails at runtime: It does not fail. The guard is harmless redundancy, but it widens the implicit-execution surface of the comprehension (extra attribute lookups, hidden truthiness check) without contributing any real safety since the inner function already validates the same condition.
